sentences.text: He told her about the mill over three evenings, in pieces, in the order he felt like telling it, which was not the order it had happened.
There had been a mill up the valley.
It had ground for a dozen villages.

There had been a road to it — a proper one, stone-based, wide enough for two carts to pass at the wide places — and it had come down off the hill, through what was now their top garden, and out over the wall towards the ford.
The mill closed in 1888.

The road was formally stopped up in 1890, which is a phrase that means somebody wrote it down somewhere, and after that the hedges were planted across it and the fields were rearranged and within a generation there was no road and within two there was no memory of a road.

"So how do you know about it?" "Because my grandmother's grandmother carried flour along it," her grandfather said, "and she told my grandmother, and my grandmother told me, and I am telling you, and that is the entire mechanism.
There is nothing clever about it." Sabela followed the boar in July, on a warm night when it did not get properly dark until after a dozen.
She did not follow him closely.
She had been told about boars, at length, by three different adults, and she had believed all of them.
She went behind at about forty metres, in trainers, on grass, with a torch she did not turn on.
He went through the hedge.
She could not.

She had to go round by the gate and along the lane and back up the far side, which took her four minutes, and she was certain she had lost him, and when she came over the rise he was standing in the middle of the Oteros' hayfield waiting.
Not for her.
She wants to be clear about that; he never once acknowledged her in the whole business.
He was waiting the way a person waits at a level crossing, facing forward, for something to be over.
Then he walked on, and she followed, and this is where it got strange.
He walked across the hayfield in a line.
Through the crop, which was standing, which he did not eat.
Out through the far hedge, where there was — she checked afterwards, in daylight, with her hands — no gap.
Along the edge of a plantation of young pines that had been planted in 2004 and that he went through as though the trees were somewhere else.
Down a bank so steep that she had to sit and slide, at a point where the bank had clearly, once, been cut into steps.
By the time they came out at the river she had stopped being frightened and started being something else that she did not have a word for at eleven and has never quite found since.
She was walking on a road.
It was not there.
There was bramble and bracken and a wire fence and a plantation and somebody's hayfield.
But her feet knew, in the way your feet know a stair in the dark, that the ground she was putting them on had been made.
